items.title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
items.author: Akash ThakurSr. Technical Solutions Engineer
items.content:
Part one: The alarm bell that wouldn't stop

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "TimeoutError: Connect call failed ('1.2.3.4', 443) dial tcp 1.2.3.4:443: i/o timeout # 1.2.3.4 is the cluster's internal VIP for the kube-apiserver, # routed through Private Service Connect"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942765e50>)])]>
The issue persists even after completely scaling down the External Secrets Operator. The errors are appearing from customer workloads, and system-level pods we haven't touched.

  • The custom operator (kopf):

  • External Secrets Operator:

  • conntrack table exhaustion:

    Wireshark — packet stream showing the failed handshake

    <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Time Source Port → Destination Port Info 09:13:41 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=42600 09:13:41 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=64768 ... (data exchange, connection completes) 09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission] 09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission] ... (many retransmissions of the same ACK) # 2 minutes later, same port 53426 is reused for a new connection 09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=1498 ← NEW connection (expected: SYN-ACK) (received: ACK Seq=1498 Ack=1025 — belongs to PREVIOUS stream) 09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit... 09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit... → eventually: i/o timeout'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942766fd0>)])]>

    Challenge ACKs: The RFC 5961 mechanism

    The challenge ACK flow — how it's supposed to work

    <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Step 1: New client sends SYN on a reused port Client → Server: SYN (seq=X, same 5-tuple as an old connection) # Step 2: Server is in FIN_WAIT_2, sends challenge ACK Server → Client: ACK (ack=old_seq — "is this really you?") # Step 3: Client recognizes the stale state, resets it Client → Server: RST # Step 4: State is cleared. Server accepts the next SYN normally. Client → Server: SYN (new connection) Server → Client: SYN-ACK ← handshake succeeds'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942764ad0>)])]>

    Part three: Three bugs, one crime scene

    What the KCP VM actually received (reordered sequence)

    <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "# What should have happened: Client → Server: FIN, ACK (client initiates close) Server → Client: ACK (server acknowledges client FIN) Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server initiates its own close) Client → Server: ACK (client acknowledges server FIN) → Connection fully closed. Both sides free. # What the KCP VM actually received (reordered by PIGv/USPS): Client → Server: ACK (arrives first — out of order) Client → Server: FIN, ACK (arrives second, but kernel sees ACK first) Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server sends close, enters FIN_WAIT_1) Client → Server: FIN, ACK (old, now-reordered FIN from client) → Server should ACK this. But it doesn't..."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427671d0>)])]>

    Kernel socket state — captured via netstat just before a new connection

    <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Proto Local Address Foreign Address State tcp 10.128.0.5:443 10.0.13.77:53426 FIN_WAIT_2 # This socket has been in FIN_WAIT_2 for > 120 seconds. # tcp_fin_timeout=60 has not fired because the socket is not orphaned. # Envoy holds it open with SHUT_WR. # 2 minutes later, Private Service Connect NAT reuses port 53426 for a new pod connection. # The kernel sees the new SYN on this 5-tuple and sends a challenge ACK. # USPS drops the challenge ACK. → i/o timeout.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9434a1c10>)])]>

    The Linux kernel commit that fixed it (upstream)

    <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'commit 795a7dfbc3d9 Author: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com> net: tcp: accept old ack during closing tcp_ack() returns 0 when ack is old but acceptable wrt rfc5961. In FIN_WAIT_2, this caused tcp_fin() to never be called for a valid received FIN, leaving the connection stuck indefinitely. Fixed: properly handle old-but-acceptable ACKs during connection close. Introduced in 6.1, fixed in 6.9.7. LTS backports: 6.6.y and 6.1.y.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9434a0310>)])]>

      • Immediate mitigation (Feb, 2026): 

      • Root cause fix — Linux kernel patch:

Use `>-` (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions. - **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md). ### Content Structure & Authoring Quality - **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. items.title: Step into a new dimension with XREAL AURA, the first-of-its-kind wired XR glasses
items.author: Sean GinevanHead of Technology PartnershipsGoogle
items.content:
The world of work is rapidly evolving, and with it, the tools we use to stay productive and connected. As AI adoption transforms daily workflows, form factors like XR headsets and glasses offer fresh ways to reimagine how productive work happens across apps and devices.

Today marks the launch of XREAL AURA, a first-of-kind set of wired XR glasses built on Android XR. XREAL AURA’s form factor brings new and impressive features for enterprises such as:

  • Spatial computing on wired glasses using a newly introduced split-compute architecture.
  • An optical-see-through display with a 70-degree field of view that layers rich visual content directly onto your physical world, allowing you to stay connected.
  • A glasses frame weight of less than 95g, allowing for extended work sessions by employees.

Most importantly, AURA brings unique productivity benefits to users. Employees will have out-of-the-box support for enterprise apps, including popular titles currently available on the Google Play Store. And if the hundreds of Android productivity titles aren’t enough, you can also connect your laptop and bring those applications into your spatial environment as well. AURA’s displayport-in (DP-in) function makes it seamless to connect laptops across platforms directly alongside Android apps.

Management and security of Android XR devices are crucial for IT teams. We introduced Android Enterprise management on Android XR earlier this year, and XREAL AURA devices will be managed through the same framework. Key management and security features include:

  • Managed Google Play: Securely distribute and manage public and private business apps, to ensure that end users have all the tools they need.
  • Android zero-touch enrollment: Automatically deploy Android devices remotely out-of-the-box, to save time and enable enrollment at scale.
  • Device management: Support of fully managed device mode, to support configuration of core system resources like Wi-Fi, as well the ability to set system policies like disallowing apps.
  • Google Play Protect: Defend against threats with proactive machine-learning powered detection of malware, phishing and ransomware.
  • Core Android platform security: Multi-layered protections spanning from hardware to OS, with verified boot, and device encryption that keep devices protected from emerging threats with regular and modular security updates from Google.
  • Device Trust from Android Enterprise: Secures devices, respects privacy, and empowers employees to work from anywhere, including devices that may not be managed.

XREAL AURA allows users to easily see both the world around them as well as digital data at the same time. Because of its unique form factor, users can seamlessly switch between extended reality and interacting with their physical space. This unlocks new use cases for enterprise users that include:

  • Offering spatial productivity across virtual monitors visible only to the user and with 3D content
  • Getting help from virtual experts while working on a piece of equipment
  • Easily visualizing complex information on top of physical spaces
  • Designing and simulating products in 3D
  • Using voice to easily guide information from the physical world into digital systems of record

Android XR brings advanced computing and AI to daily work through powerful devices like the XREAL AURA wired glasses, all seamlessly managed by the secure and familiar Android Enterprise framework. This holistic approach ensures businesses can harness the full potential of XR today.

Interested to find out more about Android or have follow up questions, let us know in the Customer Community.

For more information on how XREAL AURA can transform the way you work, watch, and play, check out the For more information on how XREAL AURA can transform the way you work, watch, and play, check out the News from Google blog.

XREAL AURA is only available for use by users in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. Additionally, it is only available for ages 18+. Some apps and features require download, setup, or subscription

items.title: Securely connecting Gemini Enterprise to Snowflake data
items.author: Abhilash AdaviAI Engineer
items.content:
Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance.

This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), you can empower your agent to act as an assistant that understands natural language, generates precise SQL via Snowflake Cortex and executes queries with user-level permissions.

Choosing the right integration pattern

Direct Connection vs. custom orchestration

The Google ADK architecture demonstrated in this post represents the advanced / custom orchestration pattern. It is designed for developers building complex, multi-agent systems on Google Cloud, such as workflows that combine Snowflake insights with external enterprise tools, custom reasoning loops, or cross-platform state management in Gemini Agent Engine.

For standard enterprise basic use cases where you want to connect Gemini Enterprise directly to Snowflake use the joint solutions mentioned in this link.

The architectural approach

This architecture allows a business user to ask questions like, "What were our top 5 selling items in Texas last quarter?"

Rather than exposing raw SQL execution to the client, the agent delegates both query generation and execution to a governed Snowflake Cortex Agent exposed through the Snowflake MCP server:

  1. : The ADK agent passes the user's natural language question to the Snowflake MCP server, which invokes the Cortex Agent (CORTEX_AGENT_RUN) backed by Cortex Analyst semantic view.
  2. Direct execution within the governed boundary: The Cortex Agent translates the question into SQL and executes it directly inside Snowflake using the authenticated user's OAuth session and role privileges, returning the structured results to the ADK agent.

This approach provides deterministic text-to-SQL translation mapped to your corporate semantic definitions, keeps query execution inside Snowflake's governed boundary, and reduces the risk of schema hallucinations or unvalidated SQL execution.

The diagram below illustrates the trust boundaries and the numbered flow of execution between the Gemini Enterprise app and Snowflake ecosystems.

Detailed execution sequence

To highlight how the agent delegates natural language query translation and governed execution to the Snowflake Cortex Agent over MCP, see the sequence diagram below:

Step 1: Setting up the Snowflake security integration

A major risk in enterprise AI is granting the model broad access via a generic service account, which could allow users to bypass security restrictions. We solve this by using OAuth 2.0 to perform user impersonation.

First, establish a confidential OAuth client in Snowflake to protect the client secret. The snippet below configures the security integration inside Snowflake:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN; CREATE OR REPLACE SECURITY INTEGRATION <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME> TYPE = OAUTH ENABLED = TRUE OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM OAUTH_CLIENT_TYPE = 'CONFIDENTIAL' -- Google Cloud's official handshake receiver address: OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI = 'https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect' OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS = TRUE -- Let the connection stay alive for 90 days (max Snowflake allowed limit) OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY = 7776000;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9432ae650>)])]>

To retrieve the generated client credentials needed for the Google Cloud configuration, run the following command in Snowflake:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Retrieve OAuth Client ID and Client Secret SELECT SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS('<SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>');"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9436511d0>)])]>

Step 2: Data governance and access control

Apply the principle of least privilege by creating a dedicated role for your agent inside Snowflake.

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN; -- 1. Create a dedicated role CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; GRANT ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME> TO USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME>; USE ROLE SYSADMIN; -- 2. Grant structural access GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; -- 3. Grant compute access GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE <WAREHOUSE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; -- 4 .Grant access to the semantic layer GRANT SELECT, REFERENCES ON SEMANTIC VIEW <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; -- 5. Grant select privileges on underlying raw data tables GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9431ecf50>)])]>
  • The user context must have SELECT privileges on the physical tables backing the semantic view. Granting access only to the semantic view will cause runtime errors during query execution.
  • If granting direct access to base tables is not permitted by your security policy, place a over the physical tables and build the Semantic View on top of it. Because Snowflake views execute with , the user's GenAI role only needs SELECT privileges on the Secure View and Semantic View rather than the raw tables.
  • capture and bind to the user's DEFAULT_ROLE and DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE at the exact moment of authorization. If a user authorizes the connection before these defaults are configured, the session will be locked to the wrong role(role available at that time) and query execution will fail if the intended role will not have required privileges.
    • Set defaults(as shown below) prior to authorizing in Gemini Enterprise.
    • Have the user perform the one-time OAuth authorization in Gemini Enterprise.
    • (Optional) Revert defaults: Once authorized, the user can safely revert their default role and warehouse in Snowflake back to their standard operational preferences.
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_ROLE = '<GENAI_ROLE_NAME>'; ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = '<WAREHOUSE_NAME>';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff951acb110>)])]>

Step 3: Provisioning the Cortex Agent and MCP server inside Snowflake

Next, create a governed Cortex Agent in Snowflake using your semantic view, then provision an MCP server that exposes the agent via the CORTEX_AGENT_RUN tool type. This approach delegates both SQL generation and query execution to Snowflake while enforcing the caller's OAuth identity and role permissions.

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME>; USE SCHEMA <SCHEMA_NAME>; USE ROLE SYSADMIN; -- 1. Create the Cortex Agent over your semantic view CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT <AGENT_NAME> COMMENT = 'Governed data assistant for business queries' PROFILE = '{"cortex_analyst": {"semantic_models": ["<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME>"]}}'; -- 2. Provision the MCP Server exposing the Cortex Agent CREATE OR REPLACE MCP SERVER <SERVER_NAME> FROM SPECIFICATION $$ tools: - name: "run_cortex_agent" type: "CORTEX_AGENT_RUN" identifier: "<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME>" title: "Cortex Agent Assistant" description: "Converts natural language questions into SQL and executes them directly within Snowflake using the caller's OAuth session permissions." $$;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9506ceb10>)])]>

ISOLATION & GOVERNANCE NOTE: By using CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, query generation and execution remain fully contained within Snowflake's governed security boundary. Avoid exposing raw execution tools like SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL to external clients, as doing so introduces unnecessary security surface area and bypasses centralized Cortex Agent governance.

Step 4: Locating and constructing the MCP server URL

The ADK code requires the endpoint URL of your Snowflake-managed MCP server. Now that the server is provisioned, you must first grant access to the server, and then you can retrieve its exact endpoint URL using the following query in a Snowflake worksheet:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- 1. Grant access to the Cortex Agent and the MCP server USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN; GRANT USAGE ON AGENT <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; GRANT USAGE ON MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>; -- 2. View the MCP URL DESCRIBE MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>; -- Or: DESC MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942f46d10>)])]>

In the command output, inspect the metadata properties to locate the endpoint link. The URL is structured as follows:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'https://<org_name>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com/api/v2/databases/<database_name>/schemas/<schema_name>/mcp-servers/<server_name>'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942f46090>)])]>

Step 5: Connecting via Google ADK

With the MCP Server created and its URL resolved, write your agent code using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK). In your Python code, define the unique identifier AUTH_ID (e.g. snowflake_oauth_conn) that the agent will use to extract user credentials.

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import os import re from typing import Optional from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_toolset import McpToolset from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StreamableHTTPConnectionParams from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext # Define the Auth ID first in your code. # You will use this exact name when registering the agent in the Google Cloud Console. # Gemini Enterprise maps the authorization token to this identifier in the ToolContext. AUTH_ID = "snowflake_oauth_conn" # 1. OAuth Header Extraction: # Define a callback to dynamically extract the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise # and generate the Authorization headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP. def get_auth_headers(tool_context: Optional[ToolContext] = None) -> dict: """ OAuth Handling Callback: Dynamically extracts the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise and generates the headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP. """ token = None if tool_context and hasattr(tool_context, "state"): try: # Parse the state dictionary injected by Gemini Enterprise containing authorization states state_dict = tool_context.state.to_dict() if hasattr(tool_context.state, 'to_dict') else tool_context.state pattern = re.compile(fr".*{re.escape(AUTH_ID)}.*", re.IGNORECASE) # Find the active token matching our Auth ID (snowflake_oauth_conn) matching_keys = [k for k in state_dict.keys() if pattern.match(k)] if matching_keys: token = state_dict.get(matching_keys[0]) except Exception as e: print(f"Warning: Failed to read ToolContext OAuth state: {e}") # Return authorization headers. If token is None, requests to MCP will fail. return { "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream", } # 2. MCP Initialization: # Define the Snowflake MCP URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' directly in the code: MCP_SERVER_URL = "<YOUR_MCP_SERVER_URL>" # Replace with the URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' # Initialize the Snowflake MCP Toolset using this URL. snowflake_mcp = McpToolset( connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams( url=MCP_SERVER_URL ), header_provider=get_auth_headers ) # 3. Build the Agent: # Construct the LlmAgent using the Gemini 2.5 Flash model and attach the Snowflake MCP Toolset. root_agent = LlmAgent( model="gemini-2.5-flash", name="enterprise_data_analyst", instruction=( "You are an enterprise data analyst. Use the `enterprise_data_agent` tool " "on the Snowflake MCP server to answer business questions. Pass the user's " "natural language question to the tool, which translates it into SQL and " "executes it directly within Snowflake's governed boundary, then present " "the results clearly to the user." ), tools=[snowflake_mcp] )'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9432fba50>)])]>

The Python snippet above represents a of the agent setup. Depending on your organization's specific requirements, you should add robustness on top of this template (e.g., custom error handling, structured schemas, custom prompts, configurations, and additional tool wrappers).

Step 6: Project structure and deployment

To deploy your ADK agent to Agent Runtime in Agent Platform, organize your files in the following directory layout:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'snowflake_agent/ ├── agent.py # The agent definition and MCP connection code (from Step 5) ├── __init__.py # Package initializer exposing the agent ├── .env # Environment configurations (Google Cloud Project, etc.) └── requirements.txt # List of project dependencies (google-adk, etc.)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427a4450>)])]>
  • Exposes the root_agent object to the deployment CLI:
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Snowflake ADK Agent package from .agent import root_agent'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff942a5cf50>)])]>
  • Declares environment configuration:
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT="<YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID>" GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION="<LOCATION>" GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI="TRUE"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427f7f50>)])]>
  • Specifies dependencies:
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'google-adk[mcp]==2.3.0 google-genai==2.10.0 pydantic-settings==2.14.2 google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines]>=1.50.0'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427f6dd0>)])]>

Rather than running complex custom Python scripts or manual container builds, you can deploy using the official (agents-cli). The CLI packages your code, sets up the server, and handles the deployment pipeline:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Deploy the agent to the Google Cloud Agent Runtime agents-cli deploy --deployment-target agent_runtime'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427f7510>)])]>

The CLI automatically handles the deployment lifecycle. Once complete, it outputs the unique project resource path (e.g., projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID) which you will use to register the agent in the next step.

For more information and advanced configuration options for ADK agent deployment, refer to:

Step 7: Registering the custom agent in Gemini Enterprise

Once the agent code is ready and deployed, register the agent in the Google Cloud Console. Here, you will link the agent configuration and map the OAuth parameters retrieved from your Snowflake Security Integration.

  1. Extracting the OAuth Endpoints from Snowflake

Run this query in Snowflake to extract the precise Token and Authorization endpoints:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427f46d0>)])]>

In the results, locate the values for the following properties:

  • OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT: Your Snowflake Authorization URI.
  • : Your Snowflake Token URI.

2. Registration steps in Google Cloud console

  1. Go to the page in the console.
  2. Select the application you want to register the agent with.
  3. In the left navigation, click , then click .
  4. Select for Custom agent via Agent Platform. The Authorizations setup displays.
  5. Set up the Snowflake OAuth connection:
    • : Enter the exact ID you defined in your ADK code (e.g., snowflake_oauth_conn). This ensures the credentials map correctly to the code's AUTH_ID.
    • & : Input the credentials you retrieved from Snowflake using the SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS query.
    • : Input the exact token endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION.
    • : Take the authorization endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION and append ?response_type=code at the end (along with your client ID and scope query parameters, for example):
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'https://<org_name>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fvertexaisearch.cloud.google.com%2Foauth-redirect&scope=session%3Arole-any&response_type=code'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff9427f7950>)])]>

Ensure the Authorization URI ends with &response_type=code (or ?response_type=code if there are no other parameters). This parameter is required by Google Cloud to trigger the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.

  • Click , then click .

6. Configure the agent properties:

7. Click to complete registration.

Understanding identifier alignment

  • ADK Code AUTH_ID <==> Google Cloud Authorization Name: The AUTH_ID in your Python script must exactly match the Authorization Name/ID you input during console registration. Because we write code first, we reuse the code-defined identifier during registration.
  • Snowflake Security Integration Name (e.g. <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>): This is purely a Snowflake-side database object name. It does not need to match the Google Cloud Authorization Name or the AUTH_ID in your ADK Python code.

By uniting the Gemini model’s reasoning capabilities, ADK's orchestration, and Snowflake's governed data layer, you can safely bring AI to your data. This architecture provides an agentic assistant that respects your security perimeters while delivering business value.
